title: Nepal Bar Association Investigation Committee Faces Crisis - Ratopati
description: Nepal Bar Association Investigation Committee Faces Crisis  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The committee formed by the Nepal Bar Association to investigate the case of Supreme Court judges and intermediaries has fallen into crisis without even starting its work. The investigation process has become uncertain after three members, including the committee's coordinator and former Bar President Chandreshwor Shrestha, refused to be on the committee.

The Bar had formed a six-member committee to investigate the controversy after some Supreme Court judges met and communicated via SMS with intermediary Inam Sapkota, and documents were leaked linking Chief Justice Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma. The committee, formed under Shrestha's coordination, includes senior advocates Purnaman Shakya, Usha Malla Pathak, Surendra Kumar Mahato, and central member of the Bar Baburam Aryal as member-secretary. Although the committee was given a deadline of one month, 15 days have already passed without starting work.

Committee coordinator Shrestha is preparing to submit a letter to Bar President Vijayprasad Mishra on the upcoming Tuesday, refusing to be on the committee. He is stepping down as coordinator, considering the hardship of his clients, as he has many cases of his clients in the Supreme Court and would have to withdraw from arguing cases if he were on the investigation committee.

Committee member and senior advocate Purnaman Shakya has already submitted a letter to Bar President Mishra and refused to be on the committee. He stated that he could not serve on the committee as he was not consulted and would have to abandon the cases of clients he argues daily. 'After being on the investigation committee, we cannot argue cases until the investigation is complete,' Shakya told Ratopati. 'It's not just one, but talks of seven judges are coming up. After being on the investigation committee, on what moral grounds can we argue?'

Shakya argues that it is practically impossible to take statements from sitting judges, demand sources from journalists, and investigate the bank statement from America that is said to be of the Chief Justice. Recalling that the Bar had protested for more than 100 days regarding the issue of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana, Shakya said that the Bar should be in a 'watchdog' role and keep a watch, and it is not necessary for it to take the initiative to investigate judges itself. He stated that the Bar can only exert pressure if any judge has proven corruption and has not resigned, and if an investigation is to be conducted, former judges or senior retired legal experts can be appointed.

Similarly, another committee member and senior advocate Surendra Mahato stated that he had informed the Bar President on the day after the committee was formed, i.e., on Kartik 17, that he could not serve on the committee.

Mahato stated that although he does not handle the cases of Deepak Bhatta and Rohit Gupta, he is the lawyer for another case connected to the root of the controversy, and due to 'conflict of interest,' it is not appropriate for him to be on the committee. He also expressed the opinion that the Bar should not form a committee as the matter of investigating judges is the responsibility of the judiciary itself.

With half of the committee's time elapsed since its formation and the situation of three members, including the coordinator, stepping down, the relevance of the Bar's investigation committee and its future course of action have become uncertain.

title: Nepal sets up accreditation centre to ease testing and certification - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal sets up accreditation centre to ease testing and certification  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Four years after the Accreditation Act, 2022 was formulated, the government has established the Nepal Accreditation Center in Kathmandu. The move is expected to reduce the time and costs businesses incur for testing and certification, improve quality standards, and lessen dependence on foreign agencies.

The centre, located within the Department of Industry premises at Tripureshwor, was formally inaugurated on November 4 by Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister Deepak Kumar Sah.

It will function as an autonomous national authority responsible for assessing and certifying the competence of laboratories, inspection agencies, and other institutions involved in testing and quality certification, with the aim of strengthening the country's quality assurance system.

In a press statement, the Industry Ministry described the establishment of the centre as an important milestone in Nepal's industrial development and trade facilitation.

“The centre has been established with the objectives of making Nepali industries competitive, ensuring that consumers have access to quality and safe goods and services, and helping establish Nepali products in international markets,” the statement said.

The centre is also expected to facilitate international accreditation and mutual recognition arrangements to support Nepal's export trade. This would help build international confidence in the quality of Nepali products and also reduce costs as well as procedural complications for exporters, the ministry said.

With the centre's establishment, laboratories, medical laboratories, inspection agencies, and certification bodies will have a domestic institution through which to seek accreditation.

The ministry said improving the credibility of institutions that test food, pharmaceutical products, construction materials, and electrical equipment would also contribute to protecting consumers' health, safety, and interests.

“Certification issued by an accredited laboratory will be internationally recognised, which will facilitate export and import. It will certify products in a manner compatible with both Nepal Standards (NS) and the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), for instance,” said Jitendra Basnet, joint secretary at the Industry Ministry.

The centre has been established to ensure that certificates issued by Nepali labs receive international recognition, he said. In the absence of an accreditation mechanism, many countries have not been accepting certificates issued by Nepali laboratories.

“We will start the centre's work by forming a team at the joint-secretary level for now and implement the law. A political appointment will be made for the centre's leadership,” Basnet said.

Exporters have welcomed the initiative but said its effectiveness will depend on how consistently the government works to make the centre fully operational. Once functional, the centre could reduce lab testing expenses by around 20 percent, they said.

However, securing international recognition will take time.

“If the government works continuously, it will take three years for the centre to become ready to accredit laboratories. The Nepal government needs to obtain recognition from an international body; otherwise, the certification will not be internationally valid,” said Govinda Prasad Ghimire, president of the Federation of Export Entrepreneurs Nepal.

Currently, foreign buyers collect product samples from Nepal, conduct lab tests in their own countries and approve shipments only after the results meet their requirements.

Testing and transportation costs are particularly high for exporters of agricultural and herbal products, who must establish that their products are free of pesticides and meet organic standards.

“It costs a minimum of Rs500-600 to test pesticide parameters and certify whether a product is organic. Logistics are also expensive. For instance, sending a 500-gram sample to the US or European markets costs at least Rs8,000,” Ghimire said.

The government will not be able to issue internationally recognised certificates immediately, as the centre needs labs meeting ISO standards, qualified human resources, and recognition from an international accreditation body, he said.

An international accreditation body will have to inspect the centre before granting recognition. This process could take two to three years if the government works continuously, Ghimire added.

At present, lab test reports take around three weeks to arrive, he said. Ghimire is also chairman of Alternative Herbal Products Private Limited, a Kathmandu-based company that produces and exports medicinal plants, spices, and food supplements to the US, Europe, and Gulf countries.

He said the centre would help ensure the quality of both edible and non-edible products. However, he expressed concerns about the reliability of food testing currently conducted by the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control.

Exporters said that while microbial testing is currently available in Nepal, they still have to send samples abroad to determine whether products are pesticide-free and meet organic certification standards.

According to the Act, institutions seeking accreditation must apply to the centre and undergo an assessment by qualified examiners. The assessment will then be reviewed by subject-specific committees before the centre decides whether to issue an accreditation certificate.

Accreditation certificates will remain valid for three years, after which institutions must renew them. Organisations that fail to renew within the prescribed period can do so within 60 days of expiry by paying double the renewal fee. Certificates will automatically be cancelled if they are not renewed within that additional period.

The centre will also be responsible for regularly monitoring accredited institutions. It can issue warnings, suspend accreditation for up to six months or reduce the scope of accreditation if an institution violates the law or prescribed conditions. Accreditation can be revoked if an institution's activities cause serious damage.

The law also brings foreign accreditation and conformity assessment organisations under national oversight. Nepali institutions seeking accreditation from foreign agencies must obtain approval from the centre, while foreign conformity assessment organisations intending to operate in Nepal must also secure its approval.

With government approval, the centre can enter into agreements with equivalent foreign, regional, and international accreditation organisations.

The law imposes fines of up to Rs100,000 for using an accreditation logo without a valid certificate or certifying substandard products and services as meeting prescribed quality standards. Using the logo outside the approved accreditation scope can attract a fine of up to Rs75,000, while other violations can result in fines of up to Rs50,000.

The centre will be chaired by the secretary of the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies. Representatives from the ministries of agriculture, health, and education, the Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology, universities, professional organisations and the private sector will also be represented.

The government published the Accreditation Regulation in the Nepal Gazette in June to implement the Act.

The regulation prescribes an application fee of Rs10,000 for laboratories and organisations involved in reference-material production and proficiency testing seeking approval to obtain foreign accreditation. The fee is Rs15,000 for organisations involved in the certification or inspection of products, services, processes, individuals and management systems.

Organisations seeking accreditation from a foreign body must apply to the centre, submitting documents establishing the foreign organisation's legal status, authority and jurisdiction, along with reasons for seeking foreign accreditation and details of the proposed accreditation's scope.

The centre may grant approval after examining the application. Once an organisation receives accreditation from a foreign body, it must submit a copy of the certificate and documents specifying the accreditation's scope to the centre within one month.

title: Film Promotion Stunts Backfire in Nepal - Ratopati
description: Film Promotion Stunts Backfire in Nepal  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. In the Nepali film industry, the trend of adopting 'promotion stunts' to attract audience attention has been on the rise lately. However, such stunts, carried out without understanding sensitivity and subject matter, often cause more harm than good to the film. A recent example is the film 'Kakakiki'.

Towards the end of the trailer launch event held on Saturday, four to five police personnel suddenly entered the hall and took director Bikky Agarwal, along with actors Gauri Malla, Manoj Gajurel, and Shishir Wandel, into a police van. As the video went viral, curiosity grew on social media about 'Why were the artists arrested?'. After the social media buzz, the unit stated that it was not real and was a 'promotion stunt'.

Following the production unit's response, the act is now facing widespread criticism. This stunt, done for promotion of the film set to be released on November 25, is now 'backfiring'.

Such promotion stunts in Nepal are proving to be counterproductive. The recently released film 'Panch Pandav' also failed due to a stunt. Although the first look showing actress Iva Giri as Draupadi received praise, the song 'Raja Chahia Chha' caused controversy. In the song, Iva, referred to as Draupadi, was shown performing an item dance in a casino, and Haribansha Acharya, playing Yudhishthira, was shown playing cards. The depiction of a proud character like Draupadi in a 'bar dancer' style was seen as an attack on religious sanctity, leading to calls for boycott. Some chief district officers even drew the attention of the Home Ministry and showed interest in the screening. Despite the director saying, 'This is not the end, but a strong beginning,' the controversy affected the film's business.

The films 'Masterni' and 'Mami' starring actress Priyanka Karki were also affected by incorrect promotion styles. For 'Masterni', a song made with Durgesh Thapa used ambiguous lyrics and gestures like 'If you want to learn math, come home in the evening,' which were criticized for attacking the professional sensitivity of teachers. Although Priyanka apologized, the business declined, and both continue to face criticism. Similarly, for the promotion of 'Mami', her act of roaming around New Road scaring people as a ghost also received negative reactions, impacting the business.

Films by singers Ramkrishna Dhakal and Prakash Saput were also harmed by controversial statements. Dhakal's claim in a television interview during the promotion of his production 'Malati Mangale' that he drove Ravi Lamichhane away in his own car after his release from jail led to a barrage of insults calling him a 'cooperative fraud,' and the film flopped. Similarly, Prakash Saput's praise for former Prime Minister and UML Chairman KP Oli, hoping it would benefit 'Basanta,' led to the film being tagged as 'UML.' Calls for boycott were made, and the audience did not support it.

However, not all promotion stunts are unsuccessful. In 'Gauthali,' actress Simran Khadka's promotion in a rural setting around Patan carrying a basket, and actor Arun Kshetri's television interview portraying an autistic character, earned praise and benefited the business. Similarly, Dipendra Lama's directorial 'Chha Maya Chhapakai' became commercially successful with a promotion stunt involving a parody of Durgesh Thapa's Teej song 'Bich Bich Ma' filmed in a tall building in Radhe Radhe, Bhaktapur.

Looking at the overall picture, 'promotion stunts' seem to have caused harm to many.

Senior journalist and director Vijayaratna Tuladhar believes that promotion styles that are appropriate to the subject matter and are dignified are more beneficial for films than cheap popularity. Tuladhar argues that the stunt of arresting actors like Gauri Malla and Manoj Gajurel misused the country's police administration. He says, 'In film promotions, there are examples in Hollywood and Bollywood where artists have presented themselves in getups suitable to the subject matter. For instance, in the promotion of the film 'Border,' which was based on an army background, all the actors came in army uniforms. But there is no need to stage a drama or a farce as if someone is genuinely arrested without reason.'

Tuladhar states that if stunts are necessary for promotion, they should be creative. He emphasizes that if the film itself is strong, other creative methods should be adopted instead of such negative promotions. 'Such stunts do not directly benefit the film, but they bring the film into discussion and create brand awareness that this is also a film,' Tuladhar adds, 'But for the film to run and last long, the film itself must be good. Once it is released, word-of-mouth publicity actually works.' He points out that promoting a film advertised as comedy by arresting actors like criminals is contrary to the subject matter.

'A film is a show business; we have to show what we have, but we shouldn't show just anything while showing it,' Tuladhar continues. 'It is better not to engage in wrong kinds of promotion.' He stresses the need to promote the film as much as possible and adopt creative styles in it.

Senior producer Sushil Pokharel says that while stunts can be used in film promotion, attention must be paid to whether they do good or bad.

'Promotion is about informing people about the film. Scandals or stunts are added to make people aware of the film,' Pokharel says. 'But publicity is of two types: 'good publicity' and 'bad publicity.' If the publicity is good and attractive, audiences will come to the hall, but if presented in a bad way, audiences will not come.' He argues that promotion stunts can be beneficial or backfire.

'The trend of stunts, scandals, and rumors is worldwide; it did not start only in Nepal. In any film industry worldwide, creating controversy and scandals has become a kind of culture in the film line,' Pokharel adds. 'Such promotion is not unique to 'Kakakiki' in Nepal; it has been happening in Hollywood and Bollywood as well.'

However, Pokharel advises that when doing such promotions, one must think carefully whether it will attract the audience or backfire. He believes that promotions should be done thoughtfully, sending a positive message to the audience like 'Wow, how good it is.'

'I personally don't like walking around the streets like a street circus. I feel that film promotion and publicity should have a certain standard,' Pokharel added. 'My belief is that promoting by making people run around the streets is cheap publicity, and cheap publicity should not be done.'

title: Nepal Premier League Cricket: Playoff Scenarios Finalized After Sunday's Matches - Ratopati
description: Nepal Premier League Cricket: Playoff Scenarios Finalized After Sunday's Matches  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The last two league stage matches of the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) cricket were completed on Sunday. With Sunday's matches, the playoff equation has also been completed. Pokhara Avengers defeated Kathmandu Gurkhas by 55 runs, while Karnali Yaks beat Chitwan Rhinos by 24 runs.

Sunday's results gave Pokhara a happy farewell, while Sudurpaschim Royals reached the qualifiers. Kathmandu and Chitwan will compete in the eliminator.

In the second match of the day, Pokhara Avengers defeated Kathmandu Gurkhas by 55 runs. Batting first, Pokhara scored 224 runs for the loss of 3 wickets in the stipulated 20 overs. This is the highest team total in NPL history.

Pokhara's Kushal Bhurtel and Yuvraj Samra batted excellently, sharing a 186-run partnership for the second wicket. This partnership became the biggest partnership in NPL history.

Kushal narrowly missed out on a century. He scored 99 runs off 50 balls with the help of 8 sixes and 8 fours. Yuvraj contributed 89 runs off 55 balls with 5 sixes and 8 fours. Arjun Kumal was out for 17 runs.

Earlier, the record for the biggest partnership in NPL was also held by Pokhara. In the first edition, Andre Gaus and Dinesh Kharel shared an unbeaten 176-run partnership for the first wicket against Lumbini Lions.

Similarly, in the second edition of NPL earlier, Biratnagar Kings had scored 220 runs against Pokhara. This season, Pokhara had scored 217 runs against Karnali Yaks. After scoring 224 runs on Sunday, Pokhara has improved its own record.

Chasing a huge target of 225 runs, Kathmandu was all out for 169 runs in 19.5 overs. Sahil Patel scored 34, Rashid Khan 31, Sonu Devkota 29, William Bosisto 26, and Jahandad Khan 24 for Kathmandu.

Pokhara's Dinesh Kharel bowled excellently, taking 4 wickets for 18 runs in 4 overs. Bipin Khatri took 3 wickets, while Ramesh Mendis, Yuvraj Samra, and Sunny Wick took one wicket each.

With this win, Pokhara finished the league stage with 4 points from 7 matches. The win in the final match has brought some relief for Pokhara, which has failed to reach the playoffs for three consecutive editions.

After the match, Pokhara's Dinesh Kharel admitted that they could not achieve the desired results according to their preparation. He said that sharing the dressing room with world-class players and especially learning from Shakib Al Hasan was a good experience for him.

He also apologized for not being able to perform as per the expectations of the fans. He said that they would return stronger in the next edition. Kharel also hinted that he would play for Nepal Police Club in the upcoming 10th National Games.

After being defeated by Pokhara, Kathmandu Gurkhas completed the league stage in third place with 8 points from 7 matches. This result has greatly benefited Sudurpaschim Royals.

Sudurpaschim secured a place in the qualifiers by finishing second with 10 points from 7 matches. Sudurpaschim will now play against top-placed Lumbini Lions in the first qualifier.

Kathmandu captain Karan KC said that the main reason for the defeat was the inability to score runs as planned in the first 10 overs while chasing the big target set by Pokhara. He said that although they had to score runs at a fast pace from the beginning to chase targets between 220 and 226 runs, the team could not succeed in it.

Acknowledging that the game went out of their control due to the big partnership between Kushal and Yuvraj, he said that if Pokhara could have been restricted to 180 to 190 runs, they could have chased the target.

However, he said that the team's morale is good before the eliminator. Kathmandu will now play against Chitwan Rhinos in the eliminator. Karan said that there was no official information about the return of foreign player David Warner.

पहिलो १० ओभरमा योजना अनुसार रन बनाउन सकेनौँ : कप्तान करण

In the first match of Sunday, Karnali Yaks defeated Chitwan Rhinos by 24 runs. Chasing a target of 154 runs set by Karnali, Chitwan was all out for 129 runs in 19.1 overs.

Usama Mir remained unbeaten on 28 for Chitwan, while Kamil Mishra scored 25. However, other batsmen could not make significant contributions, and Chitwan could not reach the target.

Hussain Talat of Karnali bowled excellently, taking 3 wickets. Mark Watt and Pawan Sarraf took 2 wickets each, while Sompal Kami took one wicket.

Earlier, batting first after winning the toss, Karnali scored 153 runs for the loss of 8 wickets in 20 overs.

Hussain Talat of Karnali remained unbeaten on 51 off 33 balls with 2 sixes and 2 fours. Ariful Islam batted aggressively, scoring 35 runs off 15 balls with the help of 2 sixes and 4 fours. Gulshan Jha scored 18 and Pawan Sarraf scored 15.

Kamal Singh Airee, Salahuddin Khan, and Usama Mir of Chitwan took 2 wickets each. Captain Sikandar Raza and Rijan Dhakal took one wicket each.

With this win, Karnali finished the tournament in sixth place with 6 points from 7 matches. Chitwan had already reached the playoffs with 7 points.

After being defeated by Karnali, Chitwan captain Sikandar Raza said that rather than the result of the match, it was important to test the ability of new players for the eliminator.

According to him, some new players performed well in the match against Karnali. He said that they could be given opportunities in the eliminator as well.

Raza also pointed out the need to improve the pitches for the development of Nepali cricket. He was of the opinion that batting-friendly and flat pitches are necessary to compete at the international level.

हारभन्दा युवा खेलाडीको प्रदर्शन महत्त्वपूर्ण छ : सिकन्दर राजा

He said that good pitches would increase the batsmen's confidence and help bowlers develop the skill of bowling in challenging situations. He also praised the performance of Kamal Singh Airee and Rijan Dhakal.

He informed that he would be absent from some playoff matches, but did not disclose which matches he would not be able to play.

After Karnali's win, young bowler Younis Singh Thakuri said that the support and advice received from Sikandar Raza have been a great inspiration in his sports career.

According to him, Raza spent about 40 to 45 minutes giving suggestions on improving bowling and how to think in difficult game situations.

Younis Singh said that learning closely from experienced international players is a great opportunity for him. He said that this has boosted his confidence and also helped him in his way of understanding the game.

His plan is to improve his bowling ability by implementing what he has learned in the NPL in the coming days.

With all the league stage matches concluded, four teams will now compete for the title. Lumbini Lions and Sudurpaschim Royals will play in the first qualifier, and Kathmandu Gurkhas and Chitwan Rhinos will play in the eliminator.

The team that wins the first qualifier will directly reach the final. The losing team will get the opportunity to play the second qualifier. The team that wins the eliminator will play the second qualifier against the team that loses the first qualifier. The final match of the third edition of NPL will be held on November 21.

title: Nepal's Parliament: Nine Elections, Three Unfinished Terms - Ratopati
description: Nepal's Parliament: Nine Elections, Three Unfinished Terms  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. A total of 9 elections to the House of Representatives have been held in Nepal so far. From the first election in 2015 BS to the election of 2082 BS, 9 parliamentary elections have been held. The parliament formed from the 2082 election is currently in power. Of the previous 8 parliaments, 3 House of Representatives were unable to complete their full term.

A total of 9 elections have been completed in the years 2015, 2048, 2051, 2056, 2064, 2070, 2074, 2079, and 2082 BS. The term of a member of the House of Representatives (MP) elected through periodic elections is 5 years. The parliaments formed after the elections of 2015, 2046, and 2079 BS were unable to complete their full term.

2015 Election

The first election to the House of Representatives in Nepal was completed in 2015 BS. According to government data, this election was completed over 45 days from Falgun 7 to Chaitra 21, 2015 BS. 9 parties participated in the election, of which 6 parties won. Some independent members were also elected.

9 parties including Nepali Congress, Nepal Communist Party, Nepal Rastriya Gorakh Parishad, United Democratic Party, Nepal Praja Parishad (Kodalo), Nepal Praja Parishad (Halo), Terai Congress, Nepali National Congress, and Nepal Prajatantrik Mahasabha participated in the election.

Nepali Congress secured a two-thirds majority by winning 74 seats in the election held for 109 seats. According to the Election Commission's data, Nepal Communist Party won 4 seats, Nepal Rastriya Gorakh Parishad won 19 seats, United Democratic Party won 5 seats, Nepal Praja Parishad (Kodalo) won 2 seats, Nepal Praja Parishad (Halo) won 1 seat, and independent candidates won four seats.

Why couldn't it complete its term?

The parliament formed after this election could not complete its term.

Nepal's first elected parliament was dissolved by the then King Mahendra on Poush 1, 2017 BS. At that time, the leader of the Congress, which had secured a two-thirds majority, Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala, was the first elected Prime Minister.

On Poush 1, 2017 BS, the then Prime Minister Koirala, who was participating in the Nepal Tarun Dal convention taking place at Thapathali in Kathmandu, was taken into custody by the army from the program venue. Not only this, the then Speaker Krishna Prasad Bhattarai, along with Congress leaders Ganesh Man Singh, Surya Prasad Upadhyay, and other ministers and members of parliament, were arrested.

Writer Jagat Nepal mentions in his book 'First Parliament' that King Mahendra used the emergency power under Article 55 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2015 BS, to dissolve the parliament and the council of ministers and take all governance into his own hands.

After that, King Mahendra banned all political parties across the country on Poush 22, 2017 BS. As a result, multi-party democracy ended, and the partyless Panchayat system began.

When dissolving the parliament, King Mahendra addressed the nation through Radio Nepal, stating that the national unity was threatened due to party interests, corruption had increased in the country, the government had failed to maintain peace and security, economic instability had increased, and the country had been harmed in the guise of democracy, according to documents found.

General Election 2048

After the success of the People's Movement of 2046 BS, the second election to the House of Representatives was held in 2048 BS. The election for 205 seats was held on Baishakh 29, 2048 BS. 18 parties participated in the election, and 8 parties won.

Nepali Congress secured a majority in the election. Congress won 110 seats. UML became second by winning 69 seats. According to the Election Commission's data, the United People's Front won 9 seats, Nepal Sadbhavana Party won 6 seats, Rastriya Prajatantrik Party (Chand) won 3 seats, Nepal Mazdoor Kisan Party (NMKP) won 2 seats, Nepal Communist Party (Democratic) won 2 seats, Rastriya Prajatantrik Party (Thapa) won 1 candidate, and three independent candidates were elected.

The House of Representatives formed from this election also could not work for its full term. The main reason for this parliament not being able to complete its full term was the extreme internal conflict within the Congress, which was running the government after securing a majority in the election, according to documents. 36 Congress MPs remained absent, causing the policy and program of the government led by Girija Prasad Koirala to fail. Subsequently, the then Prime Minister Koirala resigned on moral grounds, dissolved the House of Representatives, and announced mid-term elections. Due to this, the parliament could not complete its term.

Reason for Controversy

There was a dispute between Congress leaders Ganesh Man Singh, then party president Krishna Prasad Bhattarai, and Prime Minister Girija Prasad Koirala. 36 MPs from Singh and Bhattarai's faction were dissatisfied with the Koirala government's working style. They rebelled and remained absent during the voting on the government's annual policy and program presented in the House of Representatives on Asar 26, 2051 BS.

As the government's policy and program could not be passed due to the absence of 36 MPs from the party, the then Prime Minister Koirala resigned from the post of Prime Minister on moral grounds on the same day and recommended mid-term elections for a new mandate by dissolving the House of Representatives.

Based on Koirala's recommendation, the then King Birendra dissolved the House of Representatives on Asar 27, 2051 BS, and announced mid-term elections. The mid-term elections were completed on Kartik 29, 2051 BS.

House of Representatives Election 2079

The eighth election to the House of Representatives in Nepal was completed on Mangsir 4, 2079 BS. Out of 78 parties registered for the election, only 12 parties in the direct election and 7 parties in the proportional representation secured a place in the House of Representatives through competition. This parliament also could not complete its full term.

In the election, Congress won 57 seats in the direct election, UML won 45, the then CPN (Maoist Center) won 18, CPN (Unified Socialist) won 10, Rastriya Swatantra Party won 7, Janata Samajwadi Party Nepal won 8, Rastriya Prajatantra Party won 7, Loktantrik Samajwadi Party won 4, Nagarik Unmukti Party won 3, Janamat Party, Nepal Mazdoor Kisan Party, and Rastriya Janamorcha won 1 seat each, while 5 independent MPs were elected.

Why couldn't it complete its full term?

No political party secured a single majority in the 2079 election. There were continuous changes in the coalition in parliament and frequent changes in government. The cycle of forming and toppling governments continued.

In this sequence, KP Sharma Oli, chairman of the UML, the second largest party, became Prime Minister on Asar 30, 081 BS, with the support of the Congress, the largest party at the time. The government led by Oli decided to completely ban 26 social media platforms including Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, X (Twitter), TikTok, and WhatsApp on Bhadra 19, 2082 BS.

On the 23rd of the same month, Gen Z demanded that the government immediately lift the complete ban on 26 social media platforms including Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, X (Twitter), TikTok, and WhatsApp, and guarantee freedom of expression. They also demanded an impartial investigation into the illegal assets of high-ranking leaders, government employees, and their families, and that those involved in corruption be brought to legal accountability. They also demanded an end to the dominance of 'Nepo Kids' in government appointments and opportunities based on political connections, and ensure opportunities based on merit. They protested demanding these things.

The government used excessive force in that protest, resulting in the deaths of 19 people on the 23rd. Subsequently, on Bhadra 24, the enraged public destroyed government and private property. As a result, Prime Minister Oli was forced to resign. After Oli resigned, President Ram Chandra Paudel appointed former Chief Justice Sushila Karki as the interim Prime Minister on Gen Z's recommendation. Karki recommended the dissolution of the House of Representatives on Bhadra 27, 2082 BS. On Karki's recommendation, President Paudel dissolved the House of Representatives and announced new elections for Fagun 21, 2082 BS.

Elections were completed on the announced date. Rastriya Swatantra Party secured a majority in the election and is currently running a single-majority government.

title: Flash Flood Warning in Nepal Came Far Too Late. How Could it be Improved? - The Maritime Executive
description: Flash Flood Warning in Nepal Came Far Too Late. How Could it be Improved?  The Maritime Executive
publisher.title: The Maritime Executive
full_article:
“The scale of the tragedy is immense and overwhelming. This is likely the greatest disaster we have seen in the Himalayas in decades. The videos we have seen show that this is a type of event that is extremely difficult to predict or issue warnings for,” says Pascal Emanuel Egli, a glaciologist and associate professor at NTNU.

Egli is an expert in geophysics and glacier hydrology. He works on numerous international projects concerning natural hazards and water resources related to permafrost, snowmelt, and glaciers.

Researcher friend lost his entire village

Egli monitored the disaster in Nepal closely after the tragedy. Updates from international research colleagues arrived in his inbox several times an hour: analyses, seismic data, new satellite photos, aerial and drone imagery, and data logs from whatever monitoring equipment remains along the riverbed.

The NTNU researcher has conducted fieldwork in the region on several occasions. He has also visited the area in Nepal that has been hardest hit. A friend and fellow researcher, who currently works abroad, is from a village that has been completely wiped out by the mudflow.

20 kilometers in seven minutes

On Wednesday 26 August, at 08:37, the disaster began at an altitude of over 5,000 meters in the Rasuwa region, along the border between Nepal and Chinese-controlled Tibet. According to Egli, the event was likely triggered when the mountain slope next to the glacier collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it.

A massive block of the glacier terminus collapsed and fell hundreds of metres straight down. The debris then surged onward and into the Trishuli River at breakneck speed.

“The flash flood raced 20 kilometers down the river course in the first seven minutes. The warning from the authorities arrived at 0900, 23 minutes after the glacier collapse. Approximately 623,000 people received an SMS alert about the approaching disaster. By then, it was far too late for many of them. The warning only reached people living furthest downstream,” says Egli.

What role did the glacier play?

The massive landslide was initially registered as an earthquake. Between 100 and 250 million cubic metres of rock, ice, and soil were set in motion. Together, they formed a wall of debris that moved at up to 170–190 kilometres per hour at its peak speed, smashing everything in its path.

“Experts are currently debating what actually triggered the disaster. The landslide itself was massive. Geological factors may be to blame. But the question also remains as to what role the glacier played,” says the NTNU researcher.

Glaciers melt, natural hazards arise

Egli has conducted fieldwork on alpine glaciers in Norway, Switzerland, Chile, Pakistan, India, and Nepal. He currently leads NTNU’s contribution to the major EU project CryoSCOPE (CRYOsphere Science Concluding in new Observations and Productive Exploitation). Researchers from nine countries and twenty research institutions are investigating the impact of climate change on hydrology, on snow and retreating glaciers, and on the natural hazards that can arise as a result.

Mountain lost its structural support

Egli explains that the Himalayan glacier in question has been retreating for years due to climate change. Part of the mountainside had been supported by the glacier for thousands of years. As the glacier melts, that support for the mountain is disappearing.

“In addition, large quantities of meltwater may have exacerbated the instability already present in the mountain.”

The third factor is permafrost, which acts much like a glue holding the rock mass together. As temperatures rise, the permafrost degrades. According to Egli, this can also reduce the mountain’s stability.

Climate and natural hazards

Drawing on field studies from Norway and Switzerland, Egli’s CryoSCOPE group aims to contribute further knowledge regarding glacial hydrology – specifically water flow from melting glaciers and outburst floods. The latter are also known by the Icelandic term jøkullaup, or Glacier Lake Outburst Floods in English. They originate from lakes formed by glacial ice, meltwater, and precipitation. Glacial lakes can drain in a matter of hours, and these outbursts can cause extensive damage as they surge downstream.

Climate-driven or geological instability?

It was not an outburst flood that caused this disaster, contrary to what many people had assumed. Egli notes that some researchers believe the event was less about climate impact and more about purely geological instability.

“Others – perhaps the majority of people – believe the timing and massive scale suggest that multiple mechanisms were at play simultaneously. There appears to be a broad consensus that melting and warming have accelerated, destabilizing the mountain massif surrounding the glacier.”

The challenge of early warning

Egli is also launching a project in collaboration with Swiss and Indian colleagues. The project will take place in Ladakh, India, with the aim of establishing a cost-effective system for monitoring and providing early warnings of natural hazards.

“The early warning technology itself often works well. However, the risk of failure increases if the scale of an event is massive. Training the local population on how the systems operate can also be a challenge,” he says.

System collapse

Researchers from Nepalese universities and research institutions raise critical questions in a situation report: “Why did we fail to foresee the risk? Why did our warning system not work? Why were the consequences for lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure so severe? And, most importantly: What could we have done differently to reduce such losses?”

Egli refers to a research forum he is part of, which reveals that while the authorities have some measures in place regarding early warning and monitoring, significant failures exist. A memo seen by Gemini states that “the system is collapsing in several ways”.

Standard SMS alerts about floods and high water levels are sent out but lack concrete advice on what people should do. Responsibility is unevenly distributed among local, regional, and national authorities.

Low trust level in researchers and authorities

Furthermore, people in local communities have little trust in either researchers or the authorities. Many openly admit to having ignored warnings in the past. Some only take action when they see for themselves that “something’s happening in the river”, or when a danger alert comes from someone they trust in the village. Many initiatives intended to improve this situation stall once external funding runs out. Training and technical maintenance are not sustained.

Much remains unknown

This region of the Himalayas alone has thousands of glaciers and glacial lakes, raising the question of what lies ahead as the planet warms.

“The number of glacial lakes has increased as glaciers retreat. This is dangerous, but fortunately we know a lot about their locations; almost all of them have been mapped. What we know less about–and need to investigate more–is the stability of the moraines damming these lakes,” Egli says.

NTNU’s glacier expert notes that there is still a lot that we do not know, like how much permafrost the moraine contains. Consequently, we don’t know if or when they might collapse. We also lack information about subglacial lakes, unstable mountain slopes and moraines that could trigger landslides.

Where did all the water come from?

The flash flood in the Himalayas carried between 100 and 250 million cubic meters of rock and ice. According to Egli, one of the mysteries is why such enormous volumes of water were released in such a short time. Why didn’t the water lose momentum when the terrain levelled out after approximately seven kilometers, instead continuing with nearly the same violent force and speed?

He speculates aloud. Perhaps part of the explanation lies in the significant drop in elevation and the fact that the meltwater originated not only from beneath the glacier but also partly from within the mountain itself. On its way down, the mass of rock and ice encountered “dead ice” – remnants of another glacier – and may have melted it.

full_article:
Repeated extreme heat events in Nepal intensify interconnected environmental, household, and socio-economic stressors that community members link to childhood adversity and mental health difficulties, according to an exploratory qualitative study.

Rising global temperatures are driving more frequent extreme heat events worldwide, threatening both physical and mental health. However, researchers noted that evidence from low-resource settings remains limited regarding how linked environmental, socio-economic, and infrastructural challenges shape children’s daily lives and wellbeing.

To investigate these dynamics, researchers conducted an exploratory descriptive qualitative study in heat-affected rural and urban communities within the Bara District of Nepal. The research team conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 participants, encompassing children, caregivers, teachers, health workers, and non-governmental organization staff, analyzing the collected accounts through reflexive thematic analysis.

Study participants perceived recurring extreme heat to compound critical environmental and material hardships. In particular, extreme temperatures intensified water scarcity, electricity unreliability, drinking water contamination, food insecurity, and unsafe housing conditions, placing substantial strain on families across the affected communities.

The study found that these severe household and material stressors were associated with heightened household tension, domestic conflict, and disrupted parenting. Community participants directly connected these strained household environments to children’s exposure to adverse experiences, including parental neglect and unsafe domestic surroundings.

During periods of extreme heat, children were described as experiencing acute physical symptoms alongside psychological challenges. Participants highlighted widespread psychological distress, reduced cognitive concentration, disrupted sleep patterns, and decreased school engagement among children during severe temperature spikes.

Socioeconomically disadvantaged households faced the steepest hurdles when attempting to cope with intense heat. Although families reported utilizing coping strategies such as behavioral adjustments, increased hydration, personal cooling practices, and community rituals, relief remained severely constrained for the poorest households.

The authors concluded that establishing heat-resilient infrastructure, expanding school- and community-based mental health support, and improving local institutional coordination could help mitigate the impacts of extreme heat on children.

The Embassy of India in Kathmandu today commemorated Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas, honouring the life and legacy of Bhagwan Birsa Munda.

On the occasion, Embassy officials joined members of various indigenous communities of Nepal in paying floral tributes to Bhagwan Birsa Munda. The programme also featured a special lecture highlighting his life and legacy.

The lecture further focused on the rich cultural heritage and traditions of indigenous communities in India and Nepal, bringing attention to the diverse cultural traditions of the two countries.
